name: Zoe Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech firms, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I play violin in a wedding string trio with two friends, mostly Saturdays from May to September. On Tuesdays I teach five beginner kids at the community centre on Mill Lane, and on quiet Saturdays I busk outside the train station. I'm honestly not the best player in the trio, I'm still working on my shifting, and I know it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment at a wedding when the bride walks in and the whole room goes quiet because of what we're playing. What wears me out is the money. Winter is dead, so I pick up café shifts, and I've got about two weeks of rent in the bank at any time. Every broken string feels like a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: a computer can't stand in a church and make an aunt cry. I'd probably post something like that in the musicians' union group, half joking. People there would agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even if AI does nothing, my life is still tight. Wedding bookings have been slipping for years because couples use playlists or a cheap DJ. The hype doesn't change my real problem, which is that I earn about half of what I need in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do now: the trio, the kids on Tuesdays, the station on Saturdays. I'd try to get two more pupils by putting a card up in the library before January. I'm not touching any AI stuff, I don't trust it and I don't see the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about five minutes, then the usual knot in my stomach comes back. The rent is due on the first whether AI is hype or not. It's the same tired feeling I have every November.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trio has been losing bookings. What does that look like in a real month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last June we had six weddings, this June we had four. One couple told our cellist Priya they'd found a playlist called 'string covers for aisles' and it was free. That's eighty pounds each we didn't get, which for me is a week of food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If winter's thin, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym went last year, so now it's eating out and new strings. I play on old strings longer than I should, and you can hear it. Then I start skipping my own lesson with my old teacher, which is the one thing that would make me better.

say: A computer **can't move** an aunt to tears in a church, so live players are fine.
Wedding work is **human work**, and couples will always want real players.
think: My **real problem** is low winter income, and that stays even if AI is hype.
Bookings are already sliding to **free playlists** and cheap DJs.
do: Keep playing the **trio**, teaching Tuesdays and busking on quiet Saturdays.
Put a card in the **library** before January to find two more pupils.
feel: Brief **relief**, then the familiar **money knot** before the first of the month.
S0.quote: One couple told our cellist Priya they'd found a playlist called 'string covers for aisles' and it was free.
fieldNote: Her worry is **already there** before AI: two weeks of rent saved and a dead winter.
She skips her **own lessons** to save money, which slows the skill she needs.
Public line is confident; privately she has watched **bookings fall** from six to four.

steps.text: Keep the trio, Tuesday kids and Saturday busking going
Pin a lesson card in the library before January
Stop buying new strings and skip eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry, out loud. I'd share every union post about tech firms training on our recordings without paying us. At work I'd tell Priya and Ruth that we have to stick together on prices and not undercut each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it eats the edges of what I do. Couples will book the trio less and use AI music for the drinks hour. Parents might use an app that listens to their kid play and corrects them, so my Tuesday lessons are at risk. The busking is the only bit no software touches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's campaign for rules on AI music, properly, not just liking posts. I'd ask the community centre to sign me up for a full year of Tuesdays instead of term by term. I'd also take more café shifts, probably two evenings a week, because I don't see myself learning the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired and a bit cornered. I'm not good at changing, I know that about myself. It feels like the world is moving and asking me to move with it, and I just want to play the violin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies, mostly, and the government for letting them take everything for free. Nobody asked my permission when they scraped every wedding video with us in the background. If there were rules, a band like ours would get paid something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take more café shifts. Is that a step away from music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a step sideways, and I hate it. Every evening at the café is an evening I'm not practising, and that's how you end up a person who used to play. Rent doesn't care.

say: Tech firms are **training on our recordings** without paying musicians.
Players should **stick together on prices** and not undercut each other.
think: AI music will take the **drinks hour** at weddings and fewer couples will book.
Practice apps could cut her **Tuesday lessons**; only busking feels untouched.
do: Join the **union campaign** for AI music rules, not just liking posts.
Ask the centre for a **full-year contract** on Tuesdays.
Add **two café evenings** a week for steady money.
feel: **Cornered** and tired, because she knows she's **slow to change**.
S1.quote: Every evening at the café is an evening I'm not practising, and that's how you end up a person who used to play.
fieldNote: Blame goes clearly to **tech firms** and lax government rules.
Her fallback is **café work**, which she sees as slowly ending her music.
She admits being **resistant** and won't try AI tools even to keep pupils.

steps.text: Sign up for the musicians' union campaign on AI music rules
Ask the community centre for a full year of Tuesday lessons
Take two extra café evening shifts each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and I'd be on the street with a sign if the union organised it. Online I'd probably post too much. I'd tell people to book real musicians while they still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the music part of my income goes almost to nothing by 2028. If AI can write and arrange anything for free, the weddings that still want live strings will pick the best trio in the region, not us. The busking might last until robots come around 2031, but who busks a robot?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd move to full-time hours at the café, or anywhere with a steady wage. I'd keep the trio for whatever bookings come, probably a handful. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a basic income, because I don't see another way for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really scared. I've got two weeks of rent and no plan B that I'm proud of. It feels like the floor is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still keep the trio going. Why hold on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I stop playing, I stop being me. Ruth, our viola player, said she'd sell her viola if it got that bad, and I couldn't even listen to her. I'd play at the station for nothing before I'd sell my violin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots three years behind the thinking AI, does the hands-on part of your work buy you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, I suppose. Standing there with a bow is the part a machine can't copy yet. But being in a room isn't worth much if nobody pays to be in it. Three years is just three years of being poorer.

say: This is **exactly what we warned** about, and she'd march with the union.
People should **book real musicians** while they still exist.
think: Her music income goes to **almost nothing** by 2028.
Only the **best trios** will get the few live bookings left.
The **three-year gap** before robots buys little if nobody pays.
do: Move to **full-time café work** or any steady wage straight away.
Keep the trio for the **few bookings** that still come.
Push at union meetings for a **basic income**.
feel: **Scared**, with no plan B and only **two weeks** of rent saved.
S2.quote: I'd play at the station for nothing before I'd sell my violin.
fieldNote: She sees **no realistic plan**, and her money runs out within weeks.
Identity is tied to the **violin**; selling it is unthinkable even when broke.
Hands-on playing gives her **three years**, but she sees no buyers for it.

steps.text: Ask the café for full-time hours straight away
Go to every union meeting and march when it's organised
Push the union to campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd have time to be organised about it. I'd tell people the government has five years and no excuse. I'd probably help the union run a 'live music matters' gig night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is time for other people, not me. The players who use the tools will do fine for a while. I'll still be the one with two weeks of rent, just with a longer runway to the same cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get onto a teaching assistant course at the college, because working with kids is the part I'm good at. I'd keep the trio going while it lasts. I'd also start putting twenty pounds a week aside, even if it means no new strings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like waiting for an exam you know you'll fail. I'd have time to worry properly, which might be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A teaching assistant course: what pulls you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Tuesday kids, honestly. One of my pupils, a boy called Sami, couldn't hold a bow in September and now plays Twinkle Twinkle with his eyes shut. A classroom still needs a person in it, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. Would you do the course if it meant learning AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but I'd probably do the course anyway. If the tools are part of it, I'd learn the minimum. I'm stubborn, not stupid.

say: The government has **five years** and **no excuse** to be unready.
She'd help run a **live music night** with the union.
think: Five years helps tool users more than her; she sees the **same cliff** later.
Her **thin savings** stay the real weak point.
do: Apply for a **teaching assistant** course at the college.
Keep the trio going while **bookings** last.
Save **twenty pounds** a week, even at the cost of strings.
feel: **Heavy** dread, like waiting for an **exam** she expects to fail.
S3.quote: One of my pupils, a boy called Sami, couldn't hold a bow in September and now plays Twinkle Twinkle with his eyes shut.
fieldNote: Five years only **delays** her fear; it doesn't calm it.
Teaching children is her **real strength**, and she sees it as a lifeline.
She'd learn **minimum AI** if a course forced it: stubborn, not stupid.

steps.text: Apply for the college teaching assistant course next autumn
Put twenty pounds a week into a savings pot
Help the union run a live music night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it right, so do it right. Pay musicians for what was taken, fund music in schools. I'd say that at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels survivable. I'd be 37 when it lands. I'd have time to get a steady job working with kids and keep playing weddings on the side. That's a life, even if it's not the one I pictured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the teaching assistant course and finish it. I'd keep the trio and the Tuesday kids. I'd try to build a cushion of one month's rent, which I've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but still uneasy. The money worry doesn't go anywhere. Ten years is long enough to feel like a real choice, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your 37-year-old self about now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the café shifts weren't the end of music. That I should have saved more in my twenties instead of buying concert tickets. And that the violin was always worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that ten years you'd do that you wouldn't do in the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast pictures, going back to lessons feels pointless. With ten years, going back to proper violin lessons and getting better still counts for something. I'd go once a week to get my shifting right.

say: Ten years is enough to **do it right**: pay musicians and fund school music.
She'd keep pressing the point at **union meetings**.
think: Ten years feels **survivable**; she'd be **37** when it lands.
A steady job with kids plus **weddings on the side** is still a life.
do: Finish the **teaching assistant** course in the first year.
Keep the **trio** and Tuesday pupils going.
Build a **one-month** rent cushion for the first time.
feel: **Calmer** than the fast pictures, but the **money worry** stays.
S4.quote: With ten years, going back to proper violin lessons and getting better still counts for something.
fieldNote: The long runway makes her want to **invest in skill** again.
Money stays **thin**, so anxiety doesn't fall away even here.
Her plan is a **steady job with kids** and music on the side.

steps.text: Finish the teaching assistant course within the year
Save until one month's rent sits in the bank
Book weekly violin lessons with her old teacher again

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question. Two years is nothing when you have two weeks of rent. What would help is a basic income or at least a fund for musicians whose work was used to train these things, and free courses so people like me can retrain without going hungry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely it is. Everyone in music acts like they're fine online, and nobody admits they're behind on rent. If you're writing this up, say that.

headlineQuote: Everyone in music acts like they're fine online, and nobody admits they're behind on rent.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old violinist** in a wedding trio, teaching beginners on Tuesdays and busking on Saturdays.
She has about **two weeks of rent** saved and works café shifts every winter.
She **never uses AI** and blames tech firms and weak government rules.
Her fear rises from anxious to **panicked** as AGI gets closer; the 2028 picture leaves her without a plan.
With ten years she would **retrain** as a teaching assistant and keep playing weddings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is nothing with two weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or a fund for musicians whose work trained AI.
**Free retraining** courses that don't leave her going hungry.
